Urmila checked her email at the cyber cafe in Jhunjhunu every evening after her shift at the cooperative bank. By August she had seven rejections for junior data analyst roles, all polite, all vague.
Her friend Rekha, who ran the photocopy counter, said, "Ask them why."
So Urmila wrote to the three recruiters who had actually interviewed her: "Could you share one thing that would have made my application stronger?" Two replied. Both said the same thing in different words. Her portfolio showed neat charts, but never said what problem they solved or what a business should do next.
She sat with her three projects that weekend. The crop price chart became: "Which week should farmers in our district sell, and why?" The bank data became: "Why do small loan customers miss payments in March?" Each got a short recommendation at the end.
In October she sent the new portfolio out. Two interview calls came in the first week.

qa.q: How many rejections had Urmila received by August?
qa.a: She had seven rejections for junior data analyst roles.

qa.q: How did Urmila likely feel about the vague rejections before asking for feedback?
qa.a: She likely felt discouraged and confused, since the rejections were polite but gave no reason.

qa.q: What else could Urmila do with the rebuilt portfolio?
qa.a: She could show it to one of the recruiters who replied and ask if it now answers their concern, to test the fix directly.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel when the interview calls come?
qa.a: Rekha would likely feel pleased and proud, since her simple 'ask them why' started the change.

grounding: Shows the person asking recruiters for feedback after rejections, learning the portfolio lacks business context and rebuilding it.

Santiago had applied to eleven product analyst jobs in Bogotá after leaving teaching, and heard back from none except with rejections. His housemate Rania found him staring at his laptop on a Sunday. "Maybe you're not meant to switch."
Santiago shook his head. "Maybe I just don't know what's wrong."
He wrote to four recruiters whose companies had interviewed him, asking for one honest sentence of feedback. Two answered. One wrote: "Your projects show you can analyse data, but not why anyone should care." The other said almost the same.
He opened his portfolio. Every project ended with a chart and nothing else. So he rewrote them. His café sales analysis now opened with the owner's question, "Should we open on Mondays?", and closed with a clear answer and its likely cost.
Three weeks later he had two interviews. In one, the interviewer said, "I liked that you started with the business problem."

qa.q: What was Santiago feeling when Rania suggested he wasn't meant to switch?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and stuck but not defeated, believing the real problem was not knowing what was wrong.

qa.q: What else could Santiago do to keep improving?
qa.a: He could ask the interviewers who liked the new version what else stood out, so feedback keeps shaping each application.

qa.q: How might Rania see Santiago's response to rejection?
qa.a: Rania may feel surprised and encouraged, seeing him treat rejections as clues instead of giving up as Rania suggested.

grounding: Shows the person asking recruiters for feedback after many rejections, learning the portfolio lacks business context, and rebuilding it.
